questions.question: Explain Spring Batch chunk-oriented processing — how it works, commit intervals, skip/retry, and when to prefer tasklet.
questions.title: Spring Batch: Chunk-Oriented Processing End-to-End
questions.direct_answer: Spring Batch **chunk-oriented processing** reads items one at a time (`ItemReader`), transforms them (`ItemProcessor`), then writes them in a **batch of N** (`ItemWriter`) inside a single transaction. The cycle is: read → process → accumulate until chunk-size → write + commit. If any step fails, the **whole chunk rolls back**; `skip` and `retry` policies let you tolerate bad records or transient failures without killing the job. Typical chunk sizes are 50-1000 for JDBC; tune based on row size and DB round-trip cost. Use **tasklets** for one-shot operations (file cleanup, stored-proc calls) where there's no natural stream of items.

interviewer_intent.testing: Chunk lifecycle, commit semantics, skip/retry vs rollback, tasklet vs chunk, performance tuning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing skip (bad record) with retry (transient failure); over-small chunk sizes; using chunk for non-streaming work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss skip buffer rewind, retry inside chunk, fault tolerance with listeners, restart semantics, stateful readers via ExecutionContext

sections.title: What Chunk-Oriented Processing Means and Why the Transaction Boundary Matters
sections.content:
A Spring Batch **step** can be one of two types: **chunk-oriented** for streaming read-process-write work, or **tasklet-based** for an arbitrary unit of work like deleting temp files or calling a stored procedure.

**Chunk flow at a glance:**
- Loop until reader returns null
- Begin transaction
- Read up to `chunk_size` items, processing each as it arrives
- Pass the buffered list to `ItemWriter.write(items)`
- Commit transaction

**Key properties of the chunk model:**
- One transaction per chunk, not per item — bulk commits keep throughput high
- Failure in any sub-step rolls back the entire chunk and reprocesses it
- Restart resumes from the last committed chunk; readers track position in `ExecutionContext`
- Skip and retry policies let you tolerate bad records or transient failures

**Basic Spring Batch 5 configuration:**

```java
@Bean
public Step processOrdersStep(JobRepository jobRepository,
                              PlatformTransactionManager txManager,
                              ItemReader<Order> reader,
                              ItemProcessor<Order, Invoice> processor,
                              ItemWriter<Invoice> writer) {
    return new StepBuilder("processOrders", jobRepository)
        .<Order, Invoice>chunk(500, txManager)
        .reader(reader)
        .processor(processor)
        .writer(writer)
        .faultTolerant()
            .skip(FlatFileParseException.class).skipLimit(100)
            .retry(TransientDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)
        .build();
}
```

sections.title: Chunk Lifecycle — Read, Process, Write, Commit
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    start["Step start"]
    start --> tx["Begin transaction for chunk"]
    tx --> read["ItemReader.read"]
    read --> nullCheck{"Item is null?"}
    nullCheck -->|yes| finish["Commit last partial chunk and finish step"]
    nullCheck -->|no| process["ItemProcessor.process"]
    process --> filter{"Processed is null?"}
    filter -->|yes| skipItem["Filter item out (silent skip)"]
    filter -->|no| buffer["Buffer item"]
    skipItem --> sizeCheck{"Chunk full?"}
    buffer --> sizeCheck
    sizeCheck -->|no| read
    sizeCheck -->|yes| write["ItemWriter.write (buffered chunk)"]
    write --> commit["Commit transaction"]
    commit --> metrics["Update StepExecution counts"]
    metrics --> tx
```

sections.title: Skip, Retry, and the Single-Item Recovery Mechanism
sections.content:
Skip and retry are configured on a `faultTolerant()` step and they interact with the transaction boundary in non-obvious ways.

**Skip — discard bad records and continue**
- For known parse, validation, or constraint errors that should not fail the entire job
- `faultTolerant().skip(FlatFileParseException.class).skipLimit(500)` allows up to 500 skips
- A `SkipListener` captures every skipped item with `onSkipInRead`, `onSkipInProcess`, `onSkipInWrite`
- Use the listener to write skipped items to a dead-letter file or Kafka topic for audit

**Retry — try again on transient failures**
- For DB deadlocks, network blips, upstream 503s
- `faultTolerant().retry(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)`
- Combine with `ExponentialBackOffPolicy` to avoid retry storms
- Retry re-invokes the failing operation up to the limit; after that, exception propagates

**The single-item recovery cycle (the part candidates miss)**
- Chunk of 100 items, write fails because of one bad row
- Spring Batch rolls back the entire chunk transaction
- Then re-reads each item one at a time, processing and writing individually
- The 99 good items succeed; the one bad item is skipped (if configured) or fails the step
- This is why processors must be idempotent — they may run twice for the same input

**Skip + retry together**
- Try the chunk; retry on transient errors first
- If all retries are exhausted and the exception is skippable, skip the individual item
- If the exception is not skippable, the step fails

```java
.faultTolerant()
    .skip(FlatFileParseException.class)
    .skip(ValidationException.class)
    .skipLimit(500)
    .listener(new SkipListener<Order, Invoice>() {
        @Override
        public void onSkipInRead(Throwable t) {
            log.warn("Skipped at read", t);
            errorQueue.send(new SkipEvent("READ", t));
        }
        @Override
        public void onSkipInProcess(Order item, Throwable t) { dlq.send(item, t); }
        @Override
        public void onSkipInWrite(Invoice item, Throwable t) { dlq.send(item, t); }
    })
    .retry(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class)
    .retryLimit(3)
    .backOffPolicy(new ExponentialBackOffPolicy())
```

**Correctness pitfalls to know**
- **Non-idempotent processors break under retry/skip** — the same item may process twice
- **Readers that don't implement `ItemStream` can't resume after skip** — extend `AbstractItemStreamItemReader`
- **Skip limit set too low** — step fails on transient data issues
- **Retry on non-transient errors** — futile retries delay real failures and waste resources

sections.title: Chunk Size Tuning, Writer Choice, and Parallelism Strategies
sections.content:
Chunk size is the single most-tuned knob in Spring Batch, but **writer choice often matters more** than chunk size itself.

**Chunk size guidelines**
- **10-50** — low memory, small rollback cost, but transaction overhead dominates
- **100-500** — typical sweet spot for JDBC loads
- **1000-5000** — higher throughput for simple writes; bigger memory footprint and rollback cost
- **>10K** — rare; usually driven by DB layer batching constraints

**How to decide empirically**
- Measure throughput at chunk sizes 100, 500, 1000, 2000
- Watch DB-side metrics: longer transactions can cause lock contention
- Memory: `chunk_size × avg_item_size` must fit comfortably in heap
- Failure cost: larger chunk means more work redone on rollback

**Writer choice — often more impactful than chunk size**
- **`JdbcBatchItemWriter`** — uses `PreparedStatement.addBatch()` / `executeBatch()`; fastest for pure JDBC
- **`JpaItemWriter`** — flushes EntityManager; set `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` and `hibernate.order_inserts=true` to actually batch
- **`FlatFileItemWriter`** — buffered writer; cheap
- **`StaxEventItemWriter`** — for XML output
- **Composite writers** — split output to multiple sinks (DB + Kafka)

**Parallel processing options**

*Multi-threaded step* — same reader/writer, multiple worker threads:

```java
.taskExecutor(new SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor("batch-"))
.throttleLimit(4)
```

Requires a thread-safe reader (`SynchronizedItemStreamReader`) and disables strict restartability.

*Async processor/writer* — `AsyncItemProcessor` wraps the processor in a `Future`; `AsyncItemWriter` unwraps. Use when the processor is slow I/O (external API calls).

*Partitioning* — split input into ranges; each partition runs as its own step (locally or remotely). Best for very large jobs.

**When to use tasklet instead of chunk**
- One-shot work that's not a stream of items: delete files older than 7 days, call a stored procedure, truncate a staging table
- Compensating actions between steps
- Custom orchestration logic

```java
@Bean
public Step cleanupStep(JobRepository jobRepository, PlatformTransactionManager tx) {
    return new StepBuilder("cleanup", jobRepository)
        .tasklet((contribution, chunkContext) -> {
            Files.walk(Paths.get("/tmp/staging"))
                 .filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                 .forEach(p -> p.toFile().delete());
            return RepeatStatus.FINISHED;
        }, tx)
        .build();
}
```

**Rule of thumb** — if the work is 'process every row in X and produce Y', use chunk; if it's 'do this specific thing', use tasklet.

sections.title: Restart Semantics, Idempotency, and Production Anti-Patterns
sections.content:
**When chunk processing helps:**
- Streaming pipelines with restart from last commit boundary
- Jobs that need skip/retry tolerance for dirty data or transient failures
- Workloads where `JdbcBatchItemWriter` can collapse N inserts into one round-trip
- Audit and observability requirements via `StepExecution` counts

**When chunk processing hurts:**
- One-shot operations with no natural item — wrap in tasklet instead
- Workloads where the processor or writer has non-idempotent side effects (sending emails, charging cards)
- Very small datasets where JobRepository overhead exceeds the work
- Ultra-high-throughput pure SQL where the framework's per-chunk overhead is the bottleneck

**Watch for:**
- **Non-idempotent processors** — retry and skip both replay items; external side effects fire twice
- **Multi-threaded step + non-thread-safe reader** — data corruption; wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader`
- **Huge chunk + skip enabled** — single bad item causes massive rollback and re-processing cost
- **Retry on non-transient errors** — masks real bugs and inflates run time
- **Business logic in tasklet that should be chunk** — loses skip/retry/restart/observability
- **Chunk with non-idempotent writer** — duplicates on retry; introduce idempotency keys or outbox pattern

**Restart semantics**
- Jobs are restartable by default; `ExecutionContext` tracks reader progress
- `JdbcCursorItemReader` and `JdbcPagingItemReader` save the last offset
- `FlatFileItemReader` saves the line count
- After failure, restarting the same `JobInstance` resumes from the last committed chunk
- To force a new run of the same logical job, change `JobParameters` (use a timestamp param)

**Idempotency strategies**
- Idempotency keys in business records — UPSERT semantics in writers
- Outbox pattern — write side effects to a table inside the chunk transaction; a separate job dispatches them
- Defer side effects to a final tasklet that runs only after the chunk step completes successfully

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Chunk step** — read → process → batch-write → commit; one transaction per chunk.
- **Skip = bad record** (log and continue); **retry = transient failure** (try again).
- **Single-item recovery** after write failure — re-reads the chunk one item at a time to isolate the bad row.
- **Processors must be idempotent** — retry and skip both replay items.
- **Chunk size 100-500** typical for JDBC; tune empirically with throughput measurements.
- **`JdbcBatchItemWriter`** for fast JDBC; set `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` for JPA writers.
- **Tasklet** for one-shot work; **chunk** for streaming pipelines.
- **Parallelism** — multi-threaded step, async processor/writer, local or remote partitioning.
- **Restartability** — reader saves state in `ExecutionContext`; restart resumes at the last committed chunk.
- **Anti-patterns** — chunk=1, non-idempotent side effects, retrying non-transient errors.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch chunk-oriented processing reads items one at a time via `ItemReader`, transforms them with `ItemProcessor`, then writes them in a batch of N via `ItemWriter` inside a single transaction. If any step fails, the whole chunk rolls back; skip and retry policies let you tolerate bad records or transient failures without killing the job.

**The chunk lifecycle:**
- Begin transaction
- Read up to `chunk_size` items, processing each as it arrives
- Pass the buffered list to `ItemWriter.write(items)` in one call
- Commit transaction

**Skip vs retry:**
- **Skip** — for bad records that should be logged and ignored
- **Retry** — for transient failures like DB deadlocks or network blips
- Both require `.faultTolerant()`

**The single-item recovery cycle is the subtle part:**
- When a write fails, Spring Batch rolls back the chunk and re-reads each item individually
- The good items are written one at a time; the bad item is skipped or fails the step
- This is why processors must be idempotent — they may run twice for the same input

**Tuning advice:**
- Chunk size 100-500 for JDBC; measure to find the sweet spot
- `JdbcBatchItemWriter` usually matters more than chunk size for throughput
- For JPA writers, set `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` and `hibernate.order_inserts=true`

**Tasklet vs chunk:**
- Chunk for streaming work (process every row in X)
- Tasklet for one-shot work (delete old files, call a stored procedure)

In an interview, I'd emphasize the single-item recovery mechanism and the idempotency requirement — those are what catch candidates.

questions.question: How do you tune chunk size and design a skip policy in production? What signals tell you a chunk size is wrong, and how do you implement a custom SkipPolicy?
questions.title: Chunk Size Tuning and Custom SkipPolicy Design
questions.direct_answer: Chunk size tuning is **empirical, not theoretical** — start at 100, measure throughput at 250/500/1000/2000, and pick the largest size where memory and DB lock duration stay acceptable. Signals that the chunk size is wrong: rising **`rollback_count`** (chunks too large, hitting transient errors that force full re-read), high **transaction commit overhead** in DB metrics (chunks too small), heap pressure or OOM (chunks too large with heavy items). For skip policy, **`SimpleLimitSkipPolicy`** counts skips against a global limit; for nuanced control, implement **`SkipPolicy.shouldSkip(Throwable t, long skipCount)`** to skip on specific exception classes, allow more skips for parse errors than for DB errors, and integrate with circuit-breaker logic that fails fast when error rate exceeds a threshold.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical tuning intuition and the ability to write a non-trivial SkipPolicy that handles different exception classes differently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking a chunk size from theory ('larger is faster') without measuring; using `skipLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` and discovering the job has been silently corrupting data for weeks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss percentage-based skip tolerance, exception-specific limits, and a circuit-breaker SkipPolicy that fails fast when error rate spikes mid-job

sections.title: Chunk Size Is an Empirical Tuning Problem — Skip Policy Is a Risk-Tolerance Decision
sections.content:
Two of the most-asked production questions in Spring Batch are 'what chunk size should I use?' and 'how should my skip policy work?' Both have answers that depend on workload shape, not framework defaults.

**Chunk size** trades off three concerns: **transaction commit overhead** (smaller chunks pay it more often), **rollback cost** (larger chunks waste more work on failure), and **memory footprint** (larger chunks keep more items in heap).
- The right size is the largest value where these three constraints stay within budget — which means measuring, not guessing.
- The framework default of 10 is almost never optimal for production JDBC workloads; 100-500 is the typical sweet spot, but only measurement on your data can confirm.

**Skip policy** is fundamentally a question: **how much bad data are you willing to discard before declaring the job a failure?** For a financial reconciliation job, the answer is zero — one bad row means halt and investigate.
- For a clickstream import where 0.1% of rows have malformed timestamps, skipping a few hundred is fine.
- For a user-uploaded CSV import, a percentage-based tolerance (skip up to 5% of rows) is more honest than an absolute limit.
- A custom **`SkipPolicy`** lets you encode this risk tolerance precisely — allowing different limits for different exception classes, integrating with circuit-breaker logic, and recording skipped items to a dead-letter destination for human review.

sections.title: How to Empirically Tune Chunk Size — A Disciplined Procedure
sections.content:
Chunk size tuning follows a strict measurement-first procedure. Skip the procedure and you'll either overprovision memory or under-utilize the DB.

**Step 1 — Measure baseline at chunk size 100**
- Run the job on a representative dataset (or a realistic sample)
- Record: total duration, items per second, peak heap, average DB transaction duration, `rollback_count`
- This is your control

**Step 2 — Sweep chunk sizes 250, 500, 1000, 2000**
- Run the same job at each size; record the same metrics
- Plot items per second vs chunk size
- Most workloads show a knee in the curve — throughput rises until memory or DB lock duration becomes the constraint

**Step 3 — Watch the warning signals**
- **Rising `rollback_count`** at large chunk sizes — transient errors now force re-read of huge chunks; you've gone past the sweet spot
- **Heap pressure or full GC** — `chunk_size × avg_item_size` exceeded what the JVM can hold comfortably
- **DB lock wait time climbing** — long-running chunk transactions are blocking other workload
- **Diminishing returns** — going from 500 to 1000 gives 5% throughput but doubles memory; not worth it

**Step 4 — Pick the largest size where all signals stay green**
- For most JDBC workloads this lands at 250-1000
- For JPA writers, smaller (100-500) because EntityManager flush cost grows with chunk size
- For flat-file writers with simple records, larger (1000-5000)

**Diagnostic queries during tuning**

```sql
-- Look at chunk-level stats from the metadata
SELECT step_name, commit_count, rollback_count, read_count, write_count,
       EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_time - start_time)) AS duration_sec,
       read_count::float / EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_time - start_time)) AS rows_per_sec
FROM batch_step_execution
WHERE job_execution_id = :id
ORDER BY start_time;
```

**Common chunk-size mistakes**
- **Theoretical tuning** — picking 5000 because 'larger is faster' without measuring memory or rollback cost
- **Default of 10** — leaving the framework default in production; transaction overhead dominates
- **Mismatched JDBC batch size** — chunk size 500 with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` means 10 separate JDBC batches per chunk; align them
- **Same chunk size for every step** — read-heavy steps and write-heavy steps have different optimal sizes; tune per step

sections.title: Implementing a Production-Grade Custom SkipPolicy
Skip Policy Choices — Which One Fits Your Job
sections.content:
Pick the simplest policy that captures the actual risk tolerance.

| Policy | Best For | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| `AlwaysSkipItemSkipPolicy` | Test fixtures, dev sandboxes | Skips everything — never use in production |
| `NeverSkipItemSkipPolicy` | Financial reconciliation, zero-tolerance jobs | One bad row halts the entire job |
| `SimpleLimitSkipPolicy` | Standard 'allow N skips' jobs | One global counter — can't differentiate exception types |
| `LimitCheckingItemSkipPolicy` | Different skip limits per exception class | Verbose configuration via map |
| Custom `SkipPolicy` | Percentage tolerance, circuit-breaker, business rules | Requires careful testing |

sections.title: When to Tune, When to Leave Defaults Alone
sections.content:
**When chunk-size tuning helps:**
- Long-running jobs where a 2x throughput improvement saves real wall-clock time
- DB-bound writes where larger batches reduce round-trip cost
- Jobs where memory is plentiful and rollback cost is low

**When chunk-size tuning hurts:**
- Short jobs (< 5 minutes) — the time spent tuning exceeds the time saved
- Heap-constrained environments — large chunks cause GC pressure that erases throughput gains
- Jobs with high transient error rates — large chunks amplify rollback cost

**When custom SkipPolicy helps:**
- Different exception classes require different tolerance (parse errors common, DB errors rare)
- Percentage-based tolerance better captures business intent than absolute counts
- You need a circuit-breaker behavior to fail fast when error rate spikes

**When custom SkipPolicy hurts:**
- Simple jobs where `SimpleLimitSkipPolicy` already captures the requirement
- Code that becomes harder to reason about than the simple policy it replaces
- Stateful policy logic that breaks under multi-threaded steps (use atomic counters)

**Watch for:**
- **Tuning chunk size when writer choice is the real bottleneck** — switching to `JdbcBatchItemWriter` often beats any chunk-size change
- **Skip-everything policies in production** — `skip(Exception.class).skipLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` masks real bugs
- **Custom SkipPolicy without integration tests** — the boundary cases (exact-limit, off-by-one) are easy to get wrong
- **No dead-letter destination** — skipped items vanish; you can't audit or reprocess

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Chunk size tuning is empirical** — measure throughput at 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000 and pick the knee in the curve.
- **Three constraints to balance** — transaction commit overhead, rollback cost on failure, memory footprint.
- **Rising `rollback_count` at large chunks** — you've passed the sweet spot.
- **Align chunk size with JDBC/JPA batch size** — `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` with chunk 500 means 10 sub-batches per chunk.
- **`SimpleLimitSkipPolicy` is one global counter** — fine for simple jobs, inadequate for tiered exception tolerance.
- **Custom `SkipPolicy.shouldSkip(t, count)`** — encode per-exception limits, percentage tolerance, circuit-breaker behavior.
- **Always pair skip with a `SkipListener`** — write skipped items to a dead-letter Kafka topic, file, or table.
- **Anti-patterns** — `skipLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE)`, `skip(Exception.class)`, no dead-letter destination.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Chunk size tuning and skip policy design are two of the most-asked production Spring Batch questions, and both have answers that depend on the workload shape — not on framework defaults.

**Chunk size tuning is empirical:**
- Measure throughput at 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000 on representative data
- Pick the largest size where memory, DB lock duration, and rollback cost stay acceptable
- Watch for rising `rollback_count` at large chunks — that's the signal you've gone past the sweet spot
- For JDBC, 250-1000 is typical; for JPA writers, 100-500
- Align chunk size with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` so each chunk maps to one DB batch

**Skip policy is a risk-tolerance decision:**
- `SimpleLimitSkipPolicy` counts every skip against one global limit — fine for simple jobs
- For nuance, implement `SkipPolicy.shouldSkip(throwable, skipCount)`
- Per-exception limits — allow 1000 parse errors but only 10 DB integrity errors
- Percentage-based tolerance — fail fast if more than 5% of items are skipping; the data is too dirty to trust
- Circuit-breaker — read `StepExecution.getReadCount()` and compare against the skip count

**Always pair skip with a SkipListener:**
- Write skipped items to a dead-letter Kafka topic, file, or table
- Otherwise you've silently corrupted data and can't reprocess or audit

**Anti-patterns to call out:**
- `skipLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` masks bugs
- `skip(Exception.class)` swallows real errors like NullPointerException
- No dead-letter destination — skipped items vanish forever

In an interview, I'd emphasize that chunk tuning rewards measurement over theory, and that skip policy is fundamentally a question about how much bad data you're willing to silently discard.
